summary:
Hong Kong is a special administrative region of the People's Republic of China with its own legal system under the Basic Law. Trans rights there have been settled by court judgments rather than by statute, and no comprehensive gender recognition framework exists. As of 2026 there are no laws prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no hate crime legislation.

Identity documents can be changed on the identity card and the passport but not on the birth certificate. Historically a marker change required full sex reassignment surgery including removal of reproductive organs. A revised policy in force since April 2024 requires applicants to have undergone specified gender-affirming surgeries, mastectomy for trans men and penectomy with orchiectomy for trans women, to supply medical proof, to have lived in their identified gender for at least two years, and to be on continuous hormone therapy. The same surgical and hormonal criteria apply to trans youth seeking an identity card change. Cross-dressing in itself is not illegal.

In February 2023 the Court of Final Appeal ruled that full sex reassignment surgery must not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on the official identity card. The High Court had ruled against the trans men Henry Tse, Q and R in February 2019; Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the only objectively ascertainable criterion and rejected self-identification as producing uncertainty and arbitrariness. The men had already changed their legal gender in Britain, and counsel argued the surgery requirement was out of proportion.

On 23 July 2025 the High Court ruled in K v Secretary for Environment and Ecology that a government regulation barring trans people from public toilets matching their lived gender identity was unconstitutional under the Basic Law's right to equality. Trans people report verbal, physical and sexual abuse in public toilets.

At the border, trans woman Eliana Rubashkyn was discriminated against and sexually abused by Hong Kong airport customs officers in 2013 and subjected to an invasive body search lasting more than nine hours. She was left stateless and required assistance from UN bodies and nongovernmental organisations.

Marriage and civil unions between partners the authorities class as same-sex are not recognised. In September 2023 the Court of Final Appeal directed the government to establish an alternative recognition framework within two years while ruling that no constitutionally guaranteed right to marry exists. In July 2025 the government introduced the Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill, which would have granted limited medical decision rights covering hospital visits, shared medical information, organ donation and dealing with remains; the legislature rejected it on 19 September 2025 by 71 votes to 14, leaving such partners without recognised medical decision-making rights.

Other partner rights exist. A Court of Final Appeal ruling of 4 July 2018 in the QT case required immigration authorities to grant spousal visas to partners married or in civil unions abroad, effective from 19 September 2018, when the Director of Immigration announced favourable consideration of such applications. Joint tax filing took effect on the same date, limited domestic violence protection dates from 2009, and equal public housing rights were established by a Court of Final Appeal ruling of 26 November 2024.

A 2025 report concluded that LGBTQ people in Hong Kong face exclusion across several domains, including health and personal security.
tangentialFactors:
The surrounding case law on sexual orientation includes Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (Court of Appeal, CACV317/2005, September 2006), a judicial review of Crimes Ordinance provisions that set the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 while heterosexual acts were set at 16. The applicant, then 21 and in same-sex relationships since he was 16, argued the disparity was unjustified discrimination; the judgment examines whether facially neutral laws can breach equality guarantees and is a leading precedent on an equal age of consent. Conservative lawmakers defended the disparity as necessary to protect youth and preserve tradition.

Institutional resistance to LGBT visibility appears in several episodes. In 2007 the Broadcasting Authority ruled that an RTHK programme, Gay Lovers, was unfair, partial and biased towards homosexuality; the ruling was overturned by a court in 2008. In May 2019 a Cathay Pacific advertisement featuring a same-sex couple was banned by Airport Authority Hong Kong and the MTR Corporation and reinstated only after widespread public criticism. A December 2016 Hong Kong Free Press column described the organised backlash to HSBC's rainbow-lion installations, in which a viral local campaign framed homophobia as homegrown or foreign-imported.

Political opposition to LGBT measures comes from social conservatives, frequently with evangelical Christian ties. About 80 per cent of the 10,775 written submissions on the proposed Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill were opposed to it.
localsOnly:
A 2019 survey by the Chinese University of Hong Kong found 59 per cent agreed and 9 per cent disagreed that transgender people should be free to express their gender. A 2022 poll found 86 per cent of respondents aged 18 to 40 supported fair treatment, with younger and non-religious residents more likely to back anti-discrimination protections and same-sex marriage; acceptance of trans people correlates directly with educational level.

Family and partnership options for residents: step-child adoption has been affirmed since 2021 for couples classed as same-sex, in the Court of First Instance case AA v BB (S v KG), which granted a lesbian couple joint custody, shared care and guardianship over their two children following separation, establishing a judicial route to equal parental rights. Under Cap. 13, the Guardianship of Minors Ordinance, the Court of First Instance has full control over appointing or removing guardians. Residents holding British Nationals (Overseas) status can register civil partnerships at British consulates in 22 countries.

Trans residents carry the burden of the climate described above: they report high rates of rejection, victimisation and discrimination, social marginalisation is linked to negative mental health outcomes, and trans Hongkongers disproportionately experience moderate to severe depressive and anxiety symptoms. A 2025 report also identified exclusion in education.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 public-toilet ruling establishes a legal basis for facility access, but the sources do not describe how it is being implemented, whether it reaches government premises only or private venues as well, or what complaints mechanism exists.

Whether the September 2023 Court of Final Appeal direction to create an alternative recognition framework within two years has produced any draft instrument after the September 2025 rejection of the registered-partnerships bill is unresolved in the sources. No alternative framework has been enacted in the material available.

Hong Kong has no hate crime legislation, so no official disaggregated figures on anti-trans violence are available; the sources provide no incident counts for the jurisdiction.

The sources do not state whether the April 2024 identity card criteria have any application to visitors whose identity documents were issued elsewhere, or how a visitor's existing gender marker is handled at the border.
